text: Nowhere is the tension between growth and livability more apparent than in today's rapidly expanding cities. As urban sprawl consumes surrounding farmland and densely populated centers strain aging infrastructure, city planners face a daunting question: how can a city grow without becoming less equitable in the process? Cutting-edge technology alone will not solve this problem. Sensors and data can certainly help reduce traffic congestion and shorten the average commute, yet unless affordable housing and green space also underpin development plans, so-called smart cities risk benefiting only the wealthy. Gentrification illustrates this danger vividly: as neighborhoods are revitalized, rising costs frequently displace the very residents who gave those areas their character in the first place. Were city governments to reform zoning laws more thoughtfully, permitting a mix of income levels and amenities within the same district, such displacement might be considerably reduced. Nevertheless, overhauling decades-old regulations is rarely simple, and unforeseen obstacles inevitably crop up along the way. Cities that hope to phase out car dependency, for instance, must simultaneously invest in reliable public transport, lest congestion merely relocate rather than disappear. Ultimately, a truly livable city is not defined by its technology but by whether prosperity is shared equitably among all who call it home.
